title: Introduction to the Relational Data Model
keywords: introduction to the relational data model
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of introduction to the relational data model.
Apply relations, tuples, and attributes in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.

content.intro: Learn introduction to the relational data model through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Introduction to the Relational Data Model matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: Introduction to the Relational Data Model
content_blocks.alt_text: Three related tables show students, student_subjects, and subjects; primary keys identify rows and foreign keys link each student to subject marks.
content_blocks.caption: A relational model stores each fact in the table that owns it and connects rows with key columns.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use introduction to the relational data model to connect business meaning to table structure. A reliable relational design states what one row represents, how records are identified, and how related facts are connected without accidental duplication.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Relations, tuples, and attributes, Tables and records, Columns and their domains, Relation schemas and instances. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT s.full_name, e.subject_id, e.marks
FROM students AS s
JOIN student_subjects AS e ON e.student_id = s.student_id
ORDER BY s.student_id, e.subject_id;
content_blocks.expected_output: Each result row represents one student-subject mark; the composite key prevents duplicate enrollment pairs in the seed schema.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic relations, tuples, and attributes and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
